metadata.title: Global return-on-investment of COVID-19 vaccines in the first year of the vaccination programme: A model-based economic evaluation

paper_text_source: Staged bundle in the private papers repository: PubMed Central PMC13739145 full text (fetched via Europe PMC by the GitHub Actions sweep), 80,234 chars, no figure images
verification_changes: Nadia called Sevilla and colleagues the only other global estimate of lives saved the paper discusses; it is the only other global economic analysis, and the authors concede Watson's estimates are notably higher than several other global studies (Discussion, limitations) - added, and takeaway three and show notes corrected to match

Theo's takeaway two and show-notes takeaway two said the authors flag the 82.7%-of-GDP benefit as outside the method's range; the authors' caveat is that COVID-19 mortality risk was too large to be marginal for VSL, so reattributed accordingly

Theo said basic research behind mRNA vaccines goes back decades; the paper says nothing about mRNA research history, only that pre-pandemic basic research was excluded as sunk cost - cut the outside background
Nadia said high-income delivery is surely more expensive; the authors say delivery costs there are assumed to be higher - softened to likely
Nadia called the cost-effectiveness approach the cheaper method; it is the method that values benefits lower, not one with lower costs - reworded to lower-valuing

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hello and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo. It's Friday, so we've been over to r slash science to see what the subreddit found most interesting this week.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And what sat at the top is a health economics paper in Plos Medicine: "Global return-on-investment of Covid-nineteen vaccines in the first year of the vaccination programme: A model-based economic evaluation." The short version: the authors add up what the world spent developing and delivering Covid vaccines, set it against what the first year of vaccination is estimated to have saved, and conclude it paid back many times over.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is roughly the conclusion I'd have guessed before opening it. So why is it worth ten minutes?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Because the interesting part isn't the sign of the answer. It's how much of the size of the answer is decided by choices the authors had to make. Their headline return runs from roughly sixty to roughly eight hundred dollars back per dollar spent, depending on which of two standard valuation methods you use. Same deaths, same costs. That spread is the most useful lesson in the paper, and they report it openly.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay, more than a tenfold spread from a choice of method. Let's build up to that. Start with the costs.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The cost side is the cleaner half. Public and nonprofit research funding, corporate investment, manufacturing, and advance purchase agreements, which is governments committing to buy doses before they existed, to take the risk out of production. Then delivery: staff, cold chain, transport. All in, seventy-nine point four billion dollars over twenty twenty and twenty twenty-one, and more than half of it is those purchase agreements.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Seventy-nine billion. For the whole world?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: For the whole world. And, um, they say they deliberately counted it generously, because public data on what the money actually bought are thin. That's the right direction to err in.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Mm-hm. And the benefit side?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's where it gets model-shaped. They don't estimate deaths averted themselves. They take them wholesale from an earlier transmission model by Watson and colleagues, which simulated each country twice: once with the rollout as it actually happened, and once with no vaccines at all. The difference is the infections, hospital stays and deaths averted. That model put deaths averted in the first year at fourteen to twenty million.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So everything downstream inherits that model.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Everything. Then there are two ways to put dollars on those averted deaths and illnesses. The first is a cost-benefit analysis using the value of a statistical life. That's not the worth of a person. It's what people, in surveys and in real trade-offs, are willing to pay for a small cut in their risk of dying, scaled up to one death. The American reference figure is about ten million dollars, and they scale it to each country by income.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Wait — so a death averted in a rich country is worth more than one in a poor country?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: In this method, yes, in proportion to income. Hold onto that. The second method is a cost-effectiveness analysis. Instead of willingness to pay, you count quality-adjusted life years, which are years of life weighted by health, and price each one at roughly what that country's health system would have to spend to buy a healthy year some other way. Those prices are a fraction of income per head, so this method comes out far lower.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And both count the more tangible stuff too?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Both add averted hospital costs and lost work. And they count lost work conservatively: only the gap until a sick or deceased worker is replaced, not a lifetime of earnings.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. So give me the central claim in one sentence.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That the first year's investment in Covid vaccines returned far more than it cost, under either method and across every sensitivity analysis they ran. The cost-benefit version is the eight hundred figure; the cost-effectiveness version, with future years discounted, is the sixty.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Let me take the big one first. Eight hundred to one. What's actually inside it?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Almost entirely deaths. Virtually all of the cost-benefit return is the value of averted mortality, and the total benefit comes to about sixty-four trillion dollars.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hang on. How big is the world economy in their numbers?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: About seventy-eight trillion. So the benefit is roughly eighty-three percent of global G-D-P.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hmm. That tells you the method has left its range. A value of a statistical life is built for small changes in risk. Nobody can pay four-fifths of world output for anything.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And, credit to them, that's their own caveat. They write that Covid mortality risk in twenty twenty-one was so large that the trade-off is no longer marginal: people couldn't actually afford the sacrifice the standard figure implies. They also note it may cut the other way, because a dreaded, salient risk tends to command a higher willingness to pay. So they leave it as genuinely uncertain, which is honest.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: I'd go further. If the instrument can return a benefit the size of the world economy, I wouldn't read the eight hundred as a measurement. It's an exchange rate between deaths and dollars.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: I mostly agree. I'd call it a statement about how much people value not dying, multiplied by a very large number of deaths. It isn't wrong, but it isn't a return in the sense a finance ministry means.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is why I want the floor. What's the most hard-nosed version?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Well... the hardest-nosed is to throw out any valuation of health and keep only the cash-like items. Averted productivity losses alone come to about five hundred sixty-four billion dollars, against a total cost under eighty billion.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh — so about seven times the cost before you put any price on a life at all.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Before any price on a life. Add the hospital costs avoided and it's close to ten. The authors make this point themselves, and I think it's the most robust sentence in the paper.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That I'd believe. But the floor still stands on one model's deaths and infections. How hard should we lean on that?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Um, that's the right pressure point. The only other global economic analysis, by Sevilla and colleagues, put lives saved at four point one million, against this model's fourteen to twenty. The authors put that gap down mainly to its reliance on officially reported Covid data, which miss a lot where death registration is weak; Watson's model was fitted to excess deaths from all causes. And they concede Watson's figures run notably higher than the other global estimates of lives saved, too.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's a three- to fivefold disagreement on the single most important input.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It is, and the paper doesn't rerun its economics on the lower figure. I'd have liked that as a sensitivity analysis.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the counterfactual itself is a world with no vaccines but the same lockdowns?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Same restrictions, same behaviour, same variants. They flag that as a simplification and argue it biases them low, because in reality vaccination let countries reopen, and none of that shows up as benefit. That's an argument rather than something they modelled, but the direction seems plausible to me.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Sure. Where I'd push harder is the costs. Two things. First, delivery.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right. One figure everywhere: three dollars seventy per person vaccinated, taken from a study of lower-middle-income countries and applied to rich countries too. They say themselves that high-income delivery is likely more expensive, so this flatters the return.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And second, the clock starts in twenty twenty. Any basic research done before the pandemic is left out.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Excluded as a sunk cost. For the question "was the pandemic spending worth it", that's defensible. But they also argue for funding vaccine research before the next pandemic, and that pre-pandemic science is exactly the spending being decided. It isn't priced here.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So the denominator answers a narrower question than the discussion section asks.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeah, I'd put it that way.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: One more. The uncertainty intervals on the headline figures are tight. Are they real?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hmm. They're real for what they include. The base-case intervals carry only the transmission model's own uncertainty. When they also sample the economic inputs, the value of a statistical life, the thresholds, the quality-of-life losses, the cost-benefit range stretches from well under half the headline to nearly double it. And neither range includes the choice of death model or valuation method, which are the biggest levers of all.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's the episode eighty-four problem. In the white nationalism surveys, reversing the wording of one question moved endorsement by nine points, and no error bar on the estimate could have shown it. Here the instrument is the valuation method, and switching it moves the answer more than tenfold.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And they did run the switches, which is to their credit. Valuing life-years instead of lives, so an averted death in old age counts for less than one in middle age, cuts the cost-benefit return to less than half. Using a single global value per life-year, regardless of income, brings it to about a hundred and ninety. Still nowhere near one.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which brings back the thing you told me to hold onto. Rich countries.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right. In absolute dollars, high-income countries got by far the most, partly from early access, older populations and better vaccines, but partly because the method prices their lives higher. Scaled to income per person, the picture shifts: on averted hospital and productivity costs, low-income countries come out on top, and with one global value per life-year they show the largest relative gains. So who benefited most is, again, partly set by the yardstick.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Let me connect one more. Episode eighty-two, the rabies undercount from organ donors. What I liked there was the authors stating how wrong their key assumption would have to be to overturn them: donors would need about fourteen times the average risk. This paper never states its equivalent.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: No, though you can read it off. A return of about sixty on the lower-valuing method means costs would have to be roughly sixty times higher, or benefits that much lower, just to break even.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And nothing in the limitations is that big. Not the delivery cost, not the death model, not the sunk research.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Not individually. I'd want someone to check whether they compound, but I don't see a plausible path below one. And the data and code are public, so anyone can try.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Alright, takeaways. One: on the hardest-nosed accounting, productivity and hospital costs alone with no price on a life, the first year of Covid vaccination returned close to ten times its cost.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mm-hm.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Two: the headline returns, sixty or eight hundred, are set mainly by the valuation method, and the larger one implies a benefit worth most of the world economy. The authors themselves caution that Covid's death risk was too large for that method's marginal logic to hold.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Three: everything rests on one transmission model's counterfactual, and that model sits above the other global estimates of lives saved, one of them several times lower. On this evidence I'd believe the investment paid off. I wouldn't quote either multiple as a measured fact.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And what would you watch for?

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: The same economics rerun on the lower death estimate, with real high-income delivery costs. If it still clears one comfortably, the sign is settled.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mine is someone pricing the pre-pandemic research, so the preparedness argument gets a real denominator. The paper is in Plos Medicine, D-O-I ten dot one three seven one slash journal dot P-M-E-D dot one zero zero four seven seven two. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: See you next week.
